entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: multiple streams are exhausting. The fantasy is freedom. The reality is management. Five things to track. Five things to maintain. Five things that can break. The people who succeed with multiple streams are not the ones who chase every opportunity. They are the ones who build systems, who automate what they can, who know when to cut a stream that is draining more than it gives. More is not always better. Better is better. entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: knowing what to charge requires information—market rates, competitor pricing, client budgets. That information is not always available to young freelancers starting out. They do not know what the market will bear because they have never tested it. The only way to find out is to start charging and adjust based on feedback. Start with a number. If clients say yes too quickly, it is too low. If they all say no, it might be too high—or you might be targeting the wrong clients. The market is a conversation. Your price is the opening line. Adjust based on the response. And here is the deeper truth: the first time you name a price, it will feel wrong. Too high. Too arrogant. Too risky. That feeling is not a signal that your price is wrong. It is a signal that you have never done this before. Do it anyway. The feeling will pass. The skill will grow. The price will find its level.
entries.concern: Quick acceptance is asserted to prove a price too low, and discomfort is explained by inexperience alone.
entries.proposedWording: Treat customer response as one imperfect signal and review costs, demand, alternatives and boundaries; discomfort can have multiple causes.

If you have been taught not to talk about yourself, not to "brag," not to draw attention—the elevator pitch can feel like self-promotion, which feels like arrogance. It is not. It is clarity.
